assessment.Interference and nature of the expressio: The applicant was fined for comments posted on Instagram, so there was a clear interference with her freedom of expression (see paragraphs 5, 6 and 9). The posts concerned the existence of COVID-19 cases in the Krasnodar Region and the authorities’ reporting of the pandemic. Even if the statements were controversial or potentially misleading, they formed part of discussion on a matter of obvious public interest: public health and government action during the pandemic. Speech on such issues attracts strong protection under Article 10, especially where the State imposes sanctions capable of discouraging further participation in public debate (see no. 20007/22; no. 28232/22).

assessment.Legal basis and legitimate aim: The interference had a domestic legal basis in Article 13.15(9) of the Code of Administrative Offences, which penalised dissemination of socially important information "known to be untrue" and creating a risk to life or health (see paragraph 13). The measure also appears to have pursued a legitimate aim, namely the protection of health, and possibly prevention of disorder, in the context of COVID-19. However, the Convention issue is not the existence of a legal basis in the abstract, but whether that provision was applied with sufficient safeguards against arbitrariness. Here, the domestic courts did not convincingly establish the statutory elements of the offence, which already raises serious concerns as to foreseeability and lawfulness in practice (see no. 23158/20; no. 32525/20).

assessment.Public-interest context and narrow margi: The applicant’s publications were made from a personal/business account with 2,600 followers, and the material before the courts showed only one like and one reply (see paragraph 5). The relatively limited reach did not remove the possibility of harm, but it was highly relevant to the proportionality assessment. Moreover, her wording mixed factual assertions with speculation and opinion, for example, "Think about why our government would need this" and her reply about people being afraid to speak out (see paragraph 5). In such circumstances, the domestic courts were required to distinguish verifiable facts from value judgments and to assess whether there was a sufficient factual basis for the applicant’s remarks and whether she presented them as established truth. That careful analysis is especially necessary when the speech relates to public affairs (see no. 64569/09; no. 47621/13).

assessment.Failure to prove that the information wa: The central defect is that the courts did not prove that the applicant had disseminated information she knew to be false. She argued that her comments were based on publicly available online sources and that the existence of confirmed cases had not been officially clarified (see paragraph 7). Instead of requiring the authorities to show falsity and knowledge of falsity, the first-instance court held against her because she had not produced evidence disproving the existence of coronavirus in the region (see paragraph 8). That reasoning effectively reversed the burden of proof, despite domestic law expressly stating that a defendant is not required to prove innocence (see paragraph 12). The appeal court merely referred to regional anti-COVID regulations as proof that her statements were false (see paragraph 11), but those regulations did not answer the more specific questions whether she knowingly lied, whether she presented her comments under the guise of a reliable report, or whether the publication created a concrete risk to life or health as required by Article 13.15(9) (see paragraph 13). The absence of such findings means the domestic reasons were not relevant and sufficient within the meaning of Article 10 (see no. 32525/20; no. 28232/22).

assessment.Proportionality of the penalty and chill: The applicant received a fine of RUB 30,000, which was the minimum statutory amount but still a significant penalty for a private individual using social media to promote a small business (see paragraphs 5 and 9). Even non-custodial sanctions may have a chilling effect, particularly where imposed for participation in an ongoing public debate. That chilling effect is reinforced here by the summary reasoning of the appeal court and the failure to address the applicant’s arguments that her comments were not presented as reliable reporting and had not been shown to endanger anyone’s health or life (see paragraphs 10 and 11). In a democratic society, particularly weighty reasons are needed before punishing such online expression; those reasons were lacking in the present case (see no. 22385/03; no. 20007/22).

assessment.Overall conclusion: Although the aim of combating dangerous misinformation during a pandemic was legitimate, the domestic courts did not conduct the careful Convention-compliant assessment required under Article 10. They failed to establish the essential elements of the offence, shifted the burden onto the applicant, did not properly analyse context, form, reach, or risk, and imposed a sanction liable to deter further speech on matters of public concern (see paragraphs 7-13). The interference was therefore not shown to be necessary in a democratic society. A violation of Article 10 is likely (see no. 23158/20; no. 32525/20; no. 28232/22).
